pos: n. (want of power, means, or will)
etymology: Latin inhabilis, from in, not, and habilis, fit or able. Webster (1828) enters INABIL’ITY with five senses, from bodily weakness to want of moral power.
biblical_def: Inability is want of power to do a thing. Webster (1828) separates its kinds with care: want of bodily strength, as “the inability of a man to raise an arm or a leg”; want of means; want of understanding or skill; and, in sense 3, “Want of moral power.” Scripture uses all of them, but the one that matters for salvation is the last. Man by nature is “without strength” (Rom 5:6), and Christ says to His own disciples, “without me ye can do nothing” (Joh 15:5). Paul confesses, “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God” (2Co 3:5), and again, “to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not” (Rom 7:18). This inability is not a missing faculty. The sinner can think, choose and act; what he cannot do is love God, because he will not. That is why Webster adds that moral inability “aggravates our guilt.” The doctrine humbles every boast and drives the sinner to Christ, in whom the believer can say that his sufficiency is of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): INABILITY, want of sufficient physical power; want of adequate means; want of moral power; want of intellectual strength; want of knowledge or skill.
webster_full: INABIL'ITY, noun [Latin inhabilis; in and habilis.]
1. Want of sufficient physical power or strength; as the inability of a man to raise an arm or a leg.
2. Want of adequate means; as an inability to purchase a farm, or to fit out a ship.

3. Want of moral power. Moral inability is considered to be want of inclination, disposition or will, or a deep-rooted aversion to act, and therefore improperly so called. Moral inability aggravates our guilt.
4. Want of intellectual strength or force; as an inability to comprehend a mathematical demonstration.
5. Want of knowledge or skill; as an inability to read or write.
scriptures: Rom 5:6
For when we were yet without strength, in due time Christ died for the ungodly.
Joh 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Not that we are sufficient of ourselves to think any thing as of ourselves; but our sufficiency is of God;
Rom 7:18
For I know that in me (that is, in my flesh,) dwelleth no good thing: for to will is present with me; but how to perform that which is good I find not.
Job 26:2
How hast thou helped him that is without power? how savest thou the arm that hath no strength?
corruption_summary: The age treats every inability as a misfortune to be pitied and none as a fault to be repented of, so the sinner's will not is renamed a cannot and excused.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster kept the kinds of inability apart, and the modern mind runs them together. A man who cannot lift his arm is not to blame; a man who cannot love God is. To speak of the sinner's unbelief as though it were a disability, a wound or a condition beyond his control, is to borrow the innocence of sense 1 for the guilt of sense 3.

The opposite error denies the inability altogether and tells the sinner he has only to decide. Christ said, “without me ye can do nothing” (Joh 15:5). The gospel does not flatter a strength the sinner lacks; it announces that Christ died for those who were “without strength” (Rom 5:6).

roots_lines: Latin in-, not.

Sense 3, want of moral power, is the theological sense.

usage: want of sufficient physical power or strength

pos: n. (belief in the existence of a God)
etymology: Greek theos, God. Webster (1828) enters THE’ISM, “from Gr. God,” and sets it against both atheism and deism.
biblical_def: Theism is the belief that God exists. Webster (1828) defines it as “the belief or acknowledgment of the existence of a God, as opposed to atheism,” and then draws a line the modern reader often misses: theism “differs from deism, for although deism implies a belief in the existence of a God, yet it signifies in modern usage a denial of revelation, which theism does not.” Scripture treats the existence of God as known to every man: “the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse” (Rom 1:20). The denial is folly, not learning: “The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God” (Psa 14:1). Yet theism alone does not save. “He that cometh to God must believe that he is” (Heb 11:6), but the demons believe that much. The God of the Bible is not a bare supreme being; He is the LORD who says, “there is none else, there is no God beside me” (Isa 45:5), who has spoken, and who is known savingly only in Jesus Christ.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): THEISM, the belief or acknowledgment of the existence of a God, as opposed to atheism; distinct from deism, which denies revelation.
webster_full: The belief or acknowledgment of the existence of a God, as opposed to atheism. theism differs from deism, for although deism implies a belief in the existence of a God, yet it signifies in modern usage a denial of revelation, which theism does not.
scriptures: Rom 1:20
For the invisible things of him from the creation of the world are clearly seen, being understood by the things that are made, even his eternal power and Godhead; so that they are without excuse:
Psa 14:1
To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. They are corrupt, they have done abominable works, there is none that doeth good.
Heb 11:6
But without faith it is impossible to please him: for he that cometh to God must believe that he is, and that he is a rewarder of them that diligently seek him.
Isa 45:5
I am the LORD, and there is none else, there is no God beside me: I girded thee, though thou hast not known me:
corruption_summary: Modern usage stretches theism to cover any belief in any god, so that a vague higher power and the Triune God of Scripture are counted as one position.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster kept theism and deism apart because the difference is revelation. A god who made the world and then fell silent is not the God who spoke at Sinai and in His Son. To call every belief in a supreme being theism, and then count all theists as one camp, empties the word of the very thing that made it differ from deism.

The second corruption is to rest in theism as if it were faith. Rom 1:20 says the creation leaves men “without excuse,” not that it leaves them saved. Belief that God is must go on to the God who has spoken, and He is known only through the Son.

etymology: Greek polys, many, and theos, God. Webster (1828) enters POL’YTHEISM, “[Gr. many and God.]”
biblical_def: Polytheism is the belief in many gods. Webster (1828) defines it as “the doctrine of a plurality of gods or invisible beings superior to man, and having an agency in the government of the world.” Scripture answers it at the head of the law: “Thou shalt have no other gods before me” (Exo 20:3), and in Israel's confession: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4). The prophets mock the many gods for their many failures: “according to the number of thy cities are thy gods, O Judah” (Jer 2:28), and “all the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens” (Psa 96:5). Paul grants that there are “gods many, and lords many” in name, “But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ” (1Co 8:5-6). The gods of the heathen are “by nature ... no gods” (Gal 4:8). Polytheism divides the worship that belongs to the one living God among creatures and inventions, and the gospel calls men to “turn from these vanities unto the living God” (Act 14:15).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): POLYTHEISM, the doctrine of a plurality of gods or invisible beings superior to man, having an agency in the government of the world.
webster_full: The doctrine of a plurality of gods or invisible beings superior to man, and having an agency in the government of the world.

Jer 2:28

Psa 96:5
For all the gods of the nations are idols: but the LORD made the heavens.
But to us there is but one God, the Father, of whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord Jesus Christ, by whom are all things, and we by him.

And saying, Sirs, why do ye these things? We also are men of like passions with you, and preach unto you that ye should turn from these vanities unto the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea, and all things that are therein:
corruption_summary: The age calls polytheism a harmless diversity of spiritual paths, and practices it under new names: many truths, many powers, a god for every want.
corruption_paragraphs: Pluralism treats the gods of the nations as so many windows on one reality. Scripture calls them idols (Psa 96:5) and “no gods” (Gal 4:8). Paul did not admire Athens for its many altars; “his spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry” (Act 17:16).

Polytheism also survives where no statue stands. Whatever is trusted for rescue, feared for its power or served for its rewards takes the place Webster describes, an invisible power with “an agency in the government of the world.” Jeremiah's question still stands: “where are thy gods that thou hast made thee? let them arise, if they can save thee” (Jer 2:28).

etymology: Greek hairesis, heresy, and archos, chief. Webster (1828) enters HER’ESIARCH, “[Gr. heresy, and chief.]”
biblical_def: A heresiarch is the founder or head of a heresy. Webster (1828) defines him as “a leader in heresy; the chief of a sect of heretics.” The word is not in the Bible, but the man is. Paul warned the Ephesian elders: “Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things, to draw away disciples after them” (Act 20:30). Peter foretold “false teachers among you, who privily shall bring in damnable heresies, even denying the Lord that bought them” (2Pe 2:1). The mark of the heresiarch is in Paul's phrase: he draws disciples “after them,” after himself and not after Christ. The church's duty toward him is plain: “A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject” (Tit 3:10). The authority to judge him is the apostolic gospel, not the size of his following: “though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed” (Gal 1:8).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): HERESIARCH, a leader in heresy; the chief of a sect of heretics.

Gal 1:8

corruption_summary: The modern church has nearly lost the category: the leader of a new doctrine is called a fresh voice or a bold thinker, and the one who names him a heresiarch is called divisive.
corruption_paragraphs: Every heresy the church has fought had a man at its head, and Scripture expected it: men would arise “of your own selves” (Act 20:30). The modern habit is to judge such a man by his sincerity, his learning or his reach, and to treat the charge of heresy as a breach of charity. Scripture judges him by the gospel he preaches (Gal 1:8).

The opposite abuse is to call every disagreement heresy and every teacher one disagrees with a heresiarch. Webster's definition is narrow: the chief of a sect of heretics. The word belongs to those who lead others away from the faith once delivered, not to brethren who differ within it.

pos: n. & adj. (one who denies the Trinity)
etymology: Latin unitus, from unus, one. Webster (1828) enters UNITA’RIAN as both noun and adjective.
biblical_def: A Unitarian is one who denies the Trinity. Webster (1828) defines him exactly: “One who denies the doctrine of the trinity, and ascribes divinity to God the Father only.” He adds, “The Arian and Socinian are both comprehended in the term unitarian.” The Unitarian is right that God is one: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God is one LORD” (Deu 6:4). He errs in denying what the same Scripture says of the Son and the Spirit. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (Joh 1:1). Christ “is over all, God blessed for ever” (Rom 9:5), and “in him dwelleth all the fulness of the Godhead bodily” (Col 2:9). The church baptizes “in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost” (Mat 28:19): one name, three Persons. To ascribe divinity to the Father only is to deny the Son, and John's verdict is plain: “He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son” (1Jn 2:22).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): UNITARIAN, one who denies the doctrine of the trinity and ascribes divinity to God the Father only; the Arian and Socinian are both comprehended in the term.
webster_full: One who denies the doctrine of the trinity, and ascribes divinity to God the Father only. The Arian and Socinian are both comprehended in the term unitarian
Pertaining to Unitarians, or to the doctrine of the unity of the Godhead.

corruption_summary: The name now often means an open, creedless religion of shared values; Webster's definition reminds the reader that it began, and still stands, as a denial of the Son.
corruption_paragraphs: Webster defined the Unitarian by what he denies: the Trinity, and the divinity of the Son and the Spirit. That denial is the whole matter. A movement may grow broad, drop its creeds and welcome every opinion, but it does not thereby cease to deny the Son; it only ceases to say so.

The same denial lives under other names among groups that call Jesus a created being, a lesser god or a mode of the Father. Webster's note that “the Arian and Socinian are both comprehended in the term” is a useful test. Whatever the name on the door, a teaching that ascribes divinity to the Father only stands where Webster put the Unitarian, and Scripture says, “I and my Father are one” (Joh 10:30).
